messages.subject: Re: Model regressors for ts_par6
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nate and Young,
Thank you for the advice - before trying to implement a new model (which seems to be quite advanced for our skills, but we surely give it a try), I would like to test altering the ts_par6.r file.

We actually considered that before. However, having the hBayesDM package installed, it seems that the R folder contains .rdx and .rdb; where would we store the altered ts_par6.r file in order to run it smoothly?
Thanks.
Franziska

On Thursday, September 30, 2021 at 10:41:07 PM UTC+2 Haines, Nathaniel B. wrote:
> Re computing the prediction errors, I unfortunately do not have a ton of experience with this model and do not currently have the bandwidth to look into it in detail. That said, I can say that what you are saving is the expected value of the choice for the mf controller in your first line, and then the difference in expected value between mf and mb controllers on your second line. To save the prediction error, you would have to take the difference between the realized outcome and the expected value for each controller on that trial.
>
> As for your error message, it may be best to follow what Young described above—that is how you would fully integrate the model with the package. The methods I was describing is a sort of work-around, which seems to be giving trouble. It is hard to say without having the code myself, but I wonder if modifying the ts_par6.r script such that the regressors argument defaults to list("mf_RPE" = 2) would fix it. Then, you could source that file, and when calling the function you would do:
>
> outputALL_in_6 <- ts_par6(
> +     data = dataALL_in_corr, niter = 4000, nwarmup = 1000, nchain = 4, ncore = 4, modelRegressor = TRUE, stan_model(file = "/Users/prithasen/Summer_Project_TUM/Data/packrat/lib/x86_64-apple-darwin17.0/4.1.1/hBayesDM/stan_files/ts_par6_reg.stan"))
>
> Best,
> Nate
> From: hbayesd...@googlegroups.com <hbayesd...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of franzis...@gmail.com <franzis...@gmail.com>
> Sent: Wednesday, September 29, 2021 4:25 PM
> To: hbayesdm-users <hbayesd...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: Model regressors for ts_par6
>
> Dear Nate,
> Sorry for following up persistently:
>
> We followed the steps that you mentioned to add regressors, but we are stuck, maybe you could give us some advise.
>
> We have edited the code as in file ts_par6.stan
>
> 1. Line no. 124 and 125 we added:
> real mf_RPE[N, T]; #to initiate model regressor for model-free reward prediction error (mf_RPE)
> real mb_RPE[N, T]; #to initiate model regressor for model-based reward prediction error (mf_RPE)
>
> 2. Line no. 198 and 199 we added:
> mf_RPE[[i, t]   = v_mf[level1_choice[i, t]];   #regressor model-free reward prediction error
> mb_RPE[[i, t]   = v_mf[level1_choice[i, t]]-v_mb[level1_choice[i, t]];   #regressor model-based reward prediction error
>
> Does that make sense in terms of the code for retrieving the regressor for model free and model based (difference between model free and model based) reward prediction errors?
>
> When running the model, we then call up the new Stan-file, only requesting one regressor:
>
> Code:
> outputALL_in_6 <- ts_par6(
> +     data = dataALL_in_corr, niter = 4000, nwarmup = 1000, nchain = 4, ncore = 4, regressors = list("mf_RPE" = 2), stan_model(file = "/Users/prithasen/Summer_Project_TUM/Data/packrat/lib/x86_64-apple-darwin17.0/4.1.1/hBayesDM/stan_files/ts_par6_reg.stan"))
>
> Error message:
> Error in preprocess_func(raw_data, general_info, ...) :
>   unused argument (regressors = list(2))
>
> It seems that we are not initiating the arguments correctly? In the ts_par6.r file the regressors option is already included (regressors = NULL), so this shouldn't be the problem, or do we need to specify the regressors there? If so where do we find the file within the package?
>
> Would you have any advice on what to try further?
> Thank you!
> Franziska

Dear Young,
Please ignore my questions regarding the log likelihoods, I found them. Sorry!
F.

> On 30. Sep 2021, at 22:11, Franziska Knolle <franzis...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Young,
> thanks for explaining!
>
> I am trying to generate integrated loglikelihoods per subject to describe model fit per subject using the gng_m4. Is there a way to integrate/extract that automatically from the model?
>
> Thank you.
> Franziska
>
>
>
>
> > On 30. Sep 2021, at 18:57, wooyou...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/> <wooyou...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Franziska,
> >
> > In a hierarchical Bayesian framework, group and individual parameters are estimated simultaneously. For each individual, there's an individual posterior distribution and we can calculate its summary statistics like posterior mean (the mean of a posterior distribution) or posterior median. By default, hBayesDM calculates the means of individual posterior distributions and contain them in 'indPars'.
> >
> > Hope this helps.
> >
> > Best,
> > Young
> >
> >
> > On Thursday, September 30, 2021 at 3:02:17 AM UTC+9 franzis...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/> wrote:
> > > Thanks Minchul, those are helpful comments - and this is also indeed the strategy I would have followed. Thanks. BW.
> > >
> > > > On 29. Sep 2021, at 09:45, MCkim <minch...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hello, Franziska
> > > >
> > > > I am not a statistic person, and my comments can be wrong - I wonder what the hBayesDM developers think.
> > > > I mentioned about the group parameters because of the 'Shrinkage' in hierarchical models.
> > > > I cannot mathematically prove, but due to shrinkage one's individual parameter estimates would regress toward group mean,
> > > > rather than reflecting one's characteristic.
> > > > But hierarchical model pools  individual data so this effect makes the group parameter reliable, even though small number of subjects
> > > > (I think 30 people is enough to estimate group paratmeter)
> > > >
> > > > For the questions, I think what is important is your theory about the data.
> > > > If you think the participants data are drawn from different group parameters, I think you should fit model separately for each groups, vice versa.
> > > > OR I think you can fit both hypothesis (one group or two groups) and to Bayesian model comparison to choose winning model.
> > > >
> > > > Best wishes,
> > > > Minchul
> > > >
> > > > 2021년 9월 29일 수요일 오후 4시 20분 11초 UTC+9에 franzis...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>님이 작성:
> > > > > Hello Minchul,
> > > > > Thanks for the comment, and pointing me to the median/mode/mean differentiation. It did make it a lot clearer.
> > > > >
> > > > > I am not sure about your last comment - hBayesDM estimates individual and group parameters simultaneously, so individual parameters should be more stable as they account for the behaviour of the entire group, so it should be appropriate to use individual parameters?!
> > > > >
> > > > > This leads me to two questions/scenarios for which I would very much appreciate your comment:
> > > > > 1) When dealing with various predefined groups, would you recommend modelling them separately, to account for group inherent traits? Meaning comparison of group parameters would be appropriate. If I model groups separately, would I not bias the data, especially when the data sets are small (e.g. n=30)?
> > > > >
> > > > > 2) However when dealing with exactly the same dataset, and wanting to applying data driven clustering to investigate whether subject groups can be classified using individual group-informed parameters, then those parameters would need to be generated from one model containing no information about group (modelling all participants together)?
> > > > >
> > > > > Thank you. Best. Franziska
> > > > >
> > > > > > On 29. Sep 2021, at 07:04, MCkim <minch...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Hello,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I think the description about learning rate example is not right.
> > > > > > The way how to summarize posterior distribution to point estimate (i,e, mean median mode) has pros and cons
> > > > > > Please see https://mmeredith.net/blog/2019/Mean_median_mode.htm
> > > > > > I think you need to look for entire shape of the posterior distribution to justify using the median value.
> > > > > > I also think it is better to rather emphasize on group parameters than individual parameters, since hBayesDM uses hierarchical model
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Best wishes,
> > > > > > Minchul
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 2021년 9월 29일 수요일 오전 3시 35분 29초 UTC+9에 franzis...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>님이 작성:
> > > > > > > Hi Nate,

> > > > > > > Franziska
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > On 28. Sep 2021, at 16:05, Haines, Nathaniel B. <haine...@buckeyemail.osu.edu <http://buckeyemail.osu.edu/>> wrote:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Hi Franziska,
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > The mean/median is computed as the mean or median of the posterior distributions for each person. So, it is really just a way to summarize the parameter estimates for each person. In other words, the posterior distribution itself is unchanged whether you use the mean/median argument when fitting (Stan is estimating the full posterior distribution). You could actually compute the posterior means/medians with the fitted model parameters if interested, we only include the argument for convenience.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Let me know if that is clear!
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > Best,

> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If I understand that correctly, the mean and the median simply describes how the parameter is summarised by subject.
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > If we are thinking of learning rate for example then is it correct to assume that for the mean  this means that from trial to trial the learning rate is being updated based on the mean distribution of the past trials, where as for the median it would be the median distribution? > > > > > > > > Franziska

> > > Warm regards,

Dear Nate,
We are currently working on pushing a new model forward.

If I understand you correctly, the implementation of the mf/mbRPE should look like this:

mf_RPE[[i, t]   = (reward[i,t]) – v_mf[level1_choice[i, t]];   #regressor model-free reward prediction error

mfb_RPE[[i, t]   = (reward[i,t] – v_mf[level1_choice[i, t]]) - (reward[i,t] – v_mb[level1_choice[i, t]]);   #regressor difference between model-based and model-free reward prediction error
We are including this before the update of the level-1 choice (line 184) or would it need to be included after observing the reward (line 204). However the later would already have updated expected choice values?

Thank you very much!
Franziska

messages.body_plain:
You would need to source the .r file before calling the function, so it can be stored anywhere. e.g., run the following before calling the model:

source("path_to_your_model/ts_par6.r")

Then, the updated function will mask the hBayesDM version.

On Fri, Oct 22, 2021 at 10:55 PM Haines, Nathaniel B. <haine...@buckeyemail.osu.edu> wrote:

> Ahhh OK I think I am clear on the dilemma now. If you plan to use the person-level estimates in a secondary analysis (e.g., unsupervised clustering), then either assuming a single group or two (known/labelled) groups can negatively impact the unsupervised clustering. Is that the general idea, or is there something else I could be missing?
>
> If that is the case, then it may be best to not use any prior information (or at least, very minimal prior information). To do that, you could make the priors uniform/near uniform, or alternatively set the group-level means/SDs to specific, diffuse values as opposed to estimating them from data. Then, you can ensure that the person-level estimate are minimally regularized/pooled for use in a secondary analysis.
>
> The only real alternative would be to do it in a fully generative way, which would require simultaneously doing the clustering and person-level parameter estimation in a single model. e.g., something like assuming a mixture model as the group-level model, as opposed to assuming each person-level parameter comes from a single normal distribution. But this is rather complex and would require a great deal of custom coding in Stan.
>
> That said, I would recommend taking the first approach (making the priors uninformative/near uniform). This way, information from one person does not influence estimates from another person. To get an idea of how to modify the priors, you can do some simulations in R. e.g., for the go bias, you can choose means/SDs, draw from a normal distribution, and plot things out:
>
> hist(rnorm(100000, mu, sd))
>
> For the bounded parameters, you would need to also account for the parameter transformations. e.g., for learning rate:
>
> hist(pnorm(rnorm(100000, mu, sd)))
>
> The `pnorm` function is the same as the `Phi_approx` function in the stan code (see the transformed parameters block). Note that you can get a uniform distribution on the learning by setting the mean to 0 and sd to 1.
>
> So, overall, I think just setting mu_pr and sigma parameters to specific values that ensure the person-level parameters they represent are distributed near uniformly should give you the results that you are looking for. You can set these values by replacing the mu_pr[1-6] and sigma[1-6] variables with specific values in the transformed parameters block (e.g., following from the example using the `pnorm` function above, below I changed the group-level ep parameterization to ensure that ep is distributed uniformly across people by replacing the group-level mean and SD parameters with specific values of 0 and 1):
>
> "
> transformed parameters {
>    vector<lower=0,  upper=1>[N]  xi;
>    vector<lower=0,  upper=1>[N]  ep;
>    vector[N]  b;
>    vector[N]  pi;
>    vector<lower=0>[N]  rhoRew;
>    vector<lower=0>[N]  rhoPun;
>    for (i in 1:N) {
>      xi[i]  = Phi_approx(mu_pr[1]  + sigma[1]  * xi_pr[i]);
>      ep[i]  = Phi_approx(0 + 1 * ep_pr[i]);
>   }
>    b       = mu_pr[3]  + sigma[3]  * b_pr;  // vectorization
>    pi     = mu_pr[4]  + sigma[4]  * pi_pr;
>    rhoRew = exp(mu_pr[5]  + sigma[5]  * rhoRew_pr);
>    rhoPun = exp(mu_pr[6]  + sigma[6]  * rhoPun_pr);
> }
>
> "
>
>
> From: Franziska Knolle <franzis...@gmail.com>
> Sent: Friday, October 22, 2021 4:23 PM
> To: Haines, Nathaniel B. <haine...@buckeyemail.osu.edu>

> Dear Nate,
> Thank you for your response. Much appreciated!
>
> I does make sense to change the change the group level parameters.
> I believe you are referring to those, for the gng_m4:
>
> // hyper parameters
> mu_pr[1] ~  normal(0,  1.0);
> mu_pr[2] ~  normal(0,  1.0);
> mu_pr[3] ~  normal(0,  10.0);
> mu_pr[4] ~  normal(0,  10.0);
> mu_pr[5] ~  normal(0,  1.0);
> mu_pr[6] ~  normal(0,  1.0);
> sigma[1:2] ~  normal(0,  0.2);
> sigma[3:4] ~  cauchy(0,  1.0);
> sigma[5:6] ~  normal(0,  0.2);
>
> The mu_pr[3]/mu_pr[4] for go bias and pavlovian bias are already quite weak, does it make sense to lower the prior further, and similarly for all 6 parameters (say e.g. factor of 10) and accordingly for the the sigma? What value would correspond to a prior which has an SD say twice the observed SD?
>
>
>
> Regarding the second question, I do understand what you are saying but the problem is that if you are modelling a sample for which is drawn from different populations, say at risk individuals and healthy controls, than modelling them together and assuming a group population distribution minimises the detectable differences when comparing parameters across the groups. Classification based on the parameters is not possible as differences are two weak. A separate modelling of groups is only then possible if you actually know the different groups, but if you want to use the modelled parameters for classification of patients and controls for example and you are only assuming that there are two different groups, the modelling of for example a bimodal posterior would be more sensitive to potential systematic group differences. Therefore fitting all together, but allow the fitting to decide between different means of group distributions, would be extremely helpful.
>
> Thank you again!
> Franziska
>

If you instead fit a single model to both groups, you are assuming that there is really a single group/population. Is your intention to take one of these approaches?
